card.hook: Picture a wide-open square with people drifting across the paving and the buildings lined up behind them. That's Plaza de la Trinidad, and it's an easy first stop because everything sits right at eye level.
card.stand_here: Head for Plaza de La Trinidad and stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, then face south-east. That gives you the full width of the square with the buildings behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square in. Then switch to 1x for a more natural view. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it from where you stand to pick out one detail on the far side.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the screen, then slide it a little darker so the sky and sunlit walls keep their colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday. If the light drops, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the square facing the yellow Iglesia de la Santísima Trinidad, then turn so the church is over your shoulder. One blog suggests getting there early. For a brighter backdrop, try the colourful Palenqueras corner across from the square, with its painted balcony and mural. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.rules_and_safety: It looks like an open public square, but check local signs for any restrictions. One visitor says police patrol the area regularly and it felt pretty safe.
card.challenge: Take three shots: one wide, one at 1x with a clear subject, and one close detail like a doorway or colourful wall. Bonus points if a stranger strolls through the first one at exactly the right moment.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de la Trinidad is a town square in Cartagena, named after the church that stands on it. The middle of the square is about 37 m to the south-east of the entry point on the map. No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so plan on walking or taking whatever local transport you like.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Plaza de La Trinidad and stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, then face south-east. That gives you the full width of the square with the buildings behind it.

card.hook: Picture a big stone fortress sitting on a hill, glowering over the old town's rooftops like a very old, very patient security guard. That's the view you're after, and you can get it for free from the street.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle de la Media Luna in Getsemaní, along the old wall sections, and face east toward the hill. The fort lies to the east, about 4 minutes on foot, though the walk to its entrance may be longer.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the rooftops, the wall and the hilltop fort all fit in. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the fort's walls, and only use 0.5x if you want lots of street, because it makes the fort look small.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fort, then drag the slider down a little so the picture gets slightly darker and the sky doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when there's less glare and it's more comfortable out in the open, since the hill has very little shade. Late afternoon may suit best, as the sun should be behind you and fall on the fort.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and try 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the scene fits in. Turn around so the rooftops and the fort sit over your shoulder, and hold the phone a little high.
card.rules_and_safety: Calle de la Media Luna is a public street. The fort itself may have restricted entry and only some tunnels are open, so check on arrival or the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the fort on the upper third with the rooftops filling the bottom, and keep the horizon level. Then take one shot each at 1x, 2x and 5x and crown a winner.
card.good_to_know: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas was first called the Castillo de San Lázaro. Building began in 1639, and it was expanded in the years after under Spanish supervision and with African slave labour. It stands about 41 metres above sea level on Cerro San Lázaro, and UNESCO listed it in 1984 together with Cartagena's historic centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle de la Media Luna in Getsemaní, along the old wall sections, and face east toward the hill. The fort lies to the east, about 4 minutes on foot, though the walk to its entrance may be longer.

card.hook: Picture a line of glass and concrete towers standing shoulder to shoulder along the Caribbean, as if they all showed up early for the beach. That's Bocagrande, and the skyline is the star here.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open balcony at Plaza Bocagrande and look along the shore, out toward the Caribbean, so the towers rise along the coast on one side of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole skyline and the sea in one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the towers, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one tall building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on the lower third line, so the towers and sky get most of the picture.
card.best_time: Go for sunset, which one guide names as the best light. Arrive a little early to claim a spot at the balcony and try a few shots as the colours change.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Hotel Movich rooftop terrace, where the Bocagrande skyline sits behind you, and arrive before sunset because it gets crowded. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit above eye level, so the towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Over at the Castillo Grande pier, across the water from Bocagrande, ask a passer-by to stand back far enough to fit you and the skyline in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Check that Plaza Bocagrande is still open to the public before you go. Stay aware of your surroundings and keep your valuables secure, especially when you're busy taking photos.
card.challenge: Find the tallest tower you can, then frame it alone at 2x or 5x with sky all around it, like a skyscraper portrait.
card.good_to_know: Bocagrande gets its name from the wide channel mouth between El Laguito and the island of Tierra Bomba. A tower at the Hotel Estelar rises to 202 m and is said to be the tallest in Colombia. The district has several zones, including Castillogrande, South Bocagrande and El Lagüito, each with its own feel.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open balcony at Plaza Bocagrande and look along the shore, out toward the Caribbean, so the towers rise along the coast on one side of your frame.

card.hook: Here's the best thing about a big open square: you can step back, back, back, and fit the whole row of buildings into one frame without a stranger's head popping up in front.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, in Plaza de la Aduana, and face north-east. Take your main shot there, then shuffle a few steps left or right to change the angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to take in the whole square, and keep your phone level so the edges don't stretch. Then go to 1x for a natural view, and 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for doorways, balconies and lamps.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the buildings, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun makes hard shadows, so save it for close-up details rather than wide shots.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Christopher Columbus statue on the plaza, so the colonial facades and arcades are behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold it a bit above eye level so the buildings fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand at the western end of the plaza near the port side, facing east toward the Customs House facade, while you stand by the Columbus statue with the colonial facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access rules for the square aren't confirmed, so check any signs when you get there.
card.challenge: Catch a tiny figure crossing the open ground in your wide shot, so the square suddenly looks huge.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de la Aduana is a town square in Cartagena, and it makes an easy, quick photo stop. Because it's open, you can fit the surrounding buildings into one frame. Take a few shots from different spots, since the light changes how the buildings and ground look.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, in Plaza de la Aduana, and face north-east. Take your main shot there, then shuffle a few steps left or right to change the angle.

card.hook: Las Bóvedas is the kind of stop where you don't need a plan, just a free minute and a charged phone. It's spot number 5 on our Cartagena map, and it's easy and relaxed.
card.stand_here: Stand near Carrera 2, about 25 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole scene in, then switch to 1x for a natural view. For close details, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines to keep the verticals and horizons straight, then put the main subject on a grid crossing rather than dead centre.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the sun is lower and the light is softer and warmer. Midday sun makes bright and shaded areas clash.
card.selfie_here: Step inside the arcade and stand in the middle of the arched passageway, with the vaults and shop fronts behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x, and the yellow arches make a nicely symmetrical frame around your face.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then one close-up of a single detail with a person walking past for scale.
card.good_to_know: Las Bóvedas is spot number 5 on our Cartagena map. No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for it, so use the Navigate buttons below to get straight there. The subject is a short walk away from the phone icon.

card.hook: Bright sweets, colonial façades and a whole square of people drifting through: Plaza de los Coches is a busy, colourful scene, and you get to be part of it.
card.stand_here: Head for Calle del Arzobispado, the phone icon on the map, about 110 m west of the subject. Face east and the square opens out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square in. Switch to 1x for a calmer shot of a single building, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line a building edge up with a vertical line so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. After dark, night mode can work if you rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try beside the statue of Pedro de Heredia in the middle of the square, a popular photo spot. Or stand under the arcade of sweet stalls (Portal de los Dulces) across from the Clock Tower. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the buildings fill in behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Be careful at night, as pickpockets target tourists. Keep your belongings secure and stay alert, day or night. Check access on the day.
card.challenge: Catch a stranger crossing the square at the exact moment they're the right size to show how big the place feels.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de los Coches is a square in Cartagena. The statue in the middle is the 1937 monument to Pedro de Heredia, the city's founder. The Clock Tower stands directly behind the plaza.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Calle del Arzobispado, the phone icon on the map, about 110 m west of the subject. Face east and the square opens out in front of you.

card.hook: Plain, solid walls and one tall tower: the cathedral doesn't need to show off, and against the sky it still looks great. Pick a spot where the tower rises above the rooftops and let it do the work.
card.stand_here: Stand near Parque de Bolívar, about 50 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll have room to fit the tower in, and you can walk a little closer later for the portal and balconies.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the tower and the whole body of the church fit together. Then go to 1x for a natural view, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower top and the portal.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide the brightness down a touch (darker) so the sky stays blue and the walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people wandering into your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to Calle 36 at the corner with Calle de la Iglesia, beside Abaco Libros y Café, where the yellow cathedral facade fills the view behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the facade stays over your shoulder. Or sit by the benches near Bolívar's statue in Plaza de Bolívar, where the tower may peek through the trees behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand farther down Calle de Don Sancho, away from the cathedral, and shoot back toward it while you pose with the church behind you so the whole building fits.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working place of worship, so expect modest dress and limited visiting times inside; check the official site before you go. Calle de Don Sancho is busy with traffic, so go early in the morning and watch for cars.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands dead straight, and sneak a bit of street into the edge of the frame to show how big the cathedral is.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral went up between 1577 and 1612, replacing a modest church of wood and reeds. In 1586, while it was still being built, the English privateer Francis Drake attacked it and caused damage that delayed its completion. The tower and dome were refurbished in 1908 by Gaston Lelarge, but the main portal, balconies and cornices are original colonial work.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Parque de Bolívar, about 50 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll have room to fit the tower in, and you can walk a little closer later for the portal and balconies.

card.hook: The Iglesia de San Pedro Claver is about 64 m across, which is a lot of church to squeeze onto a phone screen. Good news: it's solid and sits clear against the sky, so it's an easy subject.
card.stand_here: Head for Calle San Juan de Dios and stand about 15 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and the church will be straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole church. If it won't fit, tap 0.5x, and if the walls start to lean, step back and go to 1x instead. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome and upper walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the walls with them, so the building stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shot, but check how the light falls on the building on the day. One blog also suggests going before 8:30 am to beat the traffic.
card.selfie_here: Go to Plaza de San Pedro Claver and stand in front of the church's main door, facing the entrance with the facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the elegant door and church sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner on Calle de la Iglesia where Calle 35 meets Calle de los Santos de Piedra and photograph you in the street, with the church and its yellow and peach tower behind you (check the street names on the map).
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship and part of a group of buildings with a cloister and museum, so entry rules and any ticketing may vary. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the walls dead straight on the gridlines, then zoom in on the dome and roofline and see if you can spot the bit that isn't original.
card.good_to_know: The church was built between 1580 and 1654 and has had three names: San Juan de Dios, then San Ignacio de Loyola from 1622, and now San Pedro Claver. The dome was removed in 1921 and replaced by Gastón Lelarge, so the roofline you see today isn't the original one. In 2022 a new mausoleum was dedicated behind the resting place of the Saint.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Calle San Juan de Dios and stand about 15 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and the church will be straight ahead of you.

card.hook: Picture a row of 18th-century cannons pointing out over the bay, with the Bocagrande high-rises sitting right behind them. That old-meets-new mix is why this fort makes such a good photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the front ramparts of the Fuerte de San Sebastián del Pastelillo, near the old cannons and the gate; the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the bay, so the stone and cannons are in front of you and the skyline is behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the walls, cannons and bay into one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Bocagrande skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or water, then slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the stone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go for golden hour, as the sun gets low, because it makes the old stone glow. It's a working venue, so you'll probably have other visitors, and maybe parked cars, in the background of some angles.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the old cannons along the high fort walls, inside the fort grounds, so the fort is right behind you. For a second option, try the pier beside the fort by the marina docks. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the fort over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Avenida Miramar in front of the entrance gate and sentry box, while you stand at the gate so they can fit you and the whole fort in one shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally fine, but professional shoots or commercial use might need permission, and please be mindful of other diners. Walking here from central Cartagena isn't recommended because of the distance and road conditions, so take a taxi or ride-share. Access to the ramparts may depend on the venue being open, so check opening hours before you go.
card.challenge: Crouch low and get a cannon, the bay and the Bocagrande skyline in one frame, then see if the cannon looks like it's guarding the skyscrapers.
card.good_to_know: The fort was built between 1741 and 1744 on the orders of Viceroy Sebastián de Eslava, and 'Pastelillo' comes from its shape, which people thought looked like a cake. It was meant to guard Cartagena against pirate ships and stop smuggling, and eight cannons remain on the second level and seven on the third. Since 1943 it has belonged to the Cartagena Fishing Club, and today it also holds a restaurant and yacht club.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the front ramparts of the Fuerte de San Sebastián del Pastelillo, near the old cannons and the gate; the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the bay, so the stone and cannons are in front of you and the skyline is behind them.

selfie_spots.why: The cannons and massive walls are named highlights of the fort, so a visitor standing among them has the fort itself behind them.

card.hook: Pale walls, a heavy stone doorway and wooden balconies hanging above it: this building looks like it has a few stories to tell, and the open square in front gives you room to catch them all.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de Bolívar, across the square from the palace front, and face south. The palace is to the south of you, so you'll be looking straight at it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and fit the whole façade in. If people or trees crowd the square and you can't step back any further, try 0.5x. Then use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the doorway and balconies.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines, so the palace stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives you gentler light and fewer people in the square than midday does.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold your phone a little high and try 0.5x so more of the building fits in. Stand with the palace over your shoulder and take a few, so you have one where you both look good.
card.rules_and_safety: Going inside the museum is ticketed, but the square and these outside views are free.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then walk closer and get a second one of just the stone doorway with the balconies above it. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The palace was completed in 1770 in Spanish Colonial style with Baroque touches. It was the seat of the Holy Office of the Inquisition in Cartagena. The tribunal was established in 1610 and sat until 1821. Today the building is the Museo Histórico de Cartagena.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de Bolívar, across the square from the palace front, and face south. The palace is to the south of you, so you'll be looking straight at it.

card.hook: A huge bronze figure is lounging in front of a coral-stone church like she owns the place, and honestly, she sort of does. The square is what makes this photo, so give it room.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de Santo Domingo, at the far western edge of the plaza, and face east toward the church facade. Move around the open square until the Botero sculpture sits in front of the church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the facade and the sculpture together. If the square is crowded, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and use zoom 2x for the tower and facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone facade, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its warm colour.
card.best_time: Go before 8:00 in the morning, when the square is nearly empty and the light is clean and flattering on the stone. Golden hour is the next best choice, and midday is the busiest time around the sculpture.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Botero 'La Gorda' sculpture in the plaza, with the church front directly behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone has it and you want more of the church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the western side of the open plaza in front of the church and shoot wide, while you pose by the sculpture.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship. If you go inside, look for posted signs about photography and keep your flash off, especially during Mass.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the sculpture is the star, then one where you pretend to be just as relaxed as she is.
card.good_to_know: The church has a coral-stone facade, and the Botero reclining bronze figure sits in front of it. Guides treat this square as the classic frame for the church. Entry is generally free through attending Mass, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de Santo Domingo, at the far western edge of the plaza, and face east toward the church facade. Move around the open square until the Botero sculpture sits in front of the church.

card.hook: Most people climb Mount la Popa for the big city view, then get stopped in their tracks by a courtyard full of white arches and hanging plants. Start there, because it's calmer and it's gorgeous.
card.stand_here: Go into the courtyard of Convento de la Popa, at the top of Mount la Popa, and stand right on the phone icon on the map. Face the arcade so the stone arches frame the plants and white walls.
card.zoom: Use 1x in the courtyard for natural-looking arches and walls. Try 0.5x to fit the whole arcade in one frame, and 2x or more for flowers or carved stone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the flowers, then slide it a little darker so the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Mid-morning or early afternoon. One guide says the garden is in full bloom then.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the flower-filled inner courtyard, next to the old well (the wishing well). Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the arcaded walls and hanging bougainvillea behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in public areas and the cloister, but follow posted signs and staff instructions, especially if a service is under way. Drones are typically restricted, so assume no drones. Don't walk up the hill, because the access road passes one of Cartagena's rougher neighbourhoods. Take a taxi instead.
card.challenge: Turn on your gridlines and line up one arch so it frames the plants and white wall, with the vertical lines dead straight. Bonus points if the bougainvillea sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: A wooden chapel went up here in 1607, and the convent followed a year later. The name La Popa comes from the building's shape, which looks like a galley with the church at the stern. Today it houses a Religious Museum, and each February pilgrims climb the hill on foot for the feast of the Virgen de la Candelaria.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go into the courtyard of Convento de la Popa, at the top of Mount la Popa, and stand right on the phone icon on the map. Face the arcade so the stone arches frame the plants and white walls.

card.hook: A bronze Simón Bolívar sits on his horse in the middle of a leafy park, and every palm tree seems to be leaning in for the photo. Take your time here, because the shade makes it a nice place to hang around.
card.stand_here: Parque de Bolívar (also called Plaza de Bolívar) in Cartagena: the phone icon on the map is right at the statue, so you don't need to walk any further. Face the horse and rider, or sit on a nearby bench and look at it from there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue framed by trees. Go to 0.5x to fit in more of the park, with the benches and paths in front. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to tighten up on the horse and rider, or to pick out the cathedral tower above the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the statue on the centre line, then tap the statue and drag the brightness slider down a little (darker) so the bronze keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Visitor numbers change through the day, so pick a quieter time if you want a clear view of the statue. For the shady fountain scene, any time the trees give good cover will do.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Bolívar statue with it behind you and the trees framing the shot, using the front camera (try 0.5x to fit more in). For a second option, pose in front of the shaded benches, where the trees make a nice backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: Vendors and people in costume may ask for payment if you photograph them, so be polite and clear if you don't want to pay. Keep your bag close while you're looking at your screen.
card.challenge: Take the statue shot, then wait a few seconds for someone to walk through and take another, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The park is open to everyone and you don't need a ticket. The bronze statue of Simón Bolívar on horseback stands at its centre. At the park's edge, the cathedral tower rises above the trees, so look for it when you want a colonial backdrop.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Parque de Bolívar (also called Plaza de Bolívar) in Cartagena: the phone icon on the map is right at the statue, so you don't need to walk any further. Face the horse and rider, or sit on a nearby bench and look at it from there.

selfie_research.notes: Sources are thin: no page gives a street-level spot with the park itself behind a visitor, so both selfie spots are the park's own statue and benches, not a vantage outside it. The ask-someone spot is a museum balcony that needs admission, and the page describes the view only, not a photo position; the passer-by would need to be inside the museum. The pages name no rules on selfie sticks or tripods for this park (one guide only suggests carrying a lightweight tripod, which is advice, not a rule). No safety point was found for this park: the only safety note (Airial) concerns a different Parque Bolívar in Bogotá, so I excluded it. card.hook: Picture a pair of giant bronze boots, one standing up and one flopped on its side, with a whole fortress looming behind them. A poet once said his city was like a pair of old boots, and Cartagena took that very literally.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Baluarte de Santo Domingo, the fortification walkway to the west, about 1.8 km away from the boots, and face east toward the monument and the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas. For the close-up, walk to the boots themselves in Getsemaní, near Media Luna, and shoot with the fortress behind them.
card.zoom: From the walkway, try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the faraway boots into the scene, and zoom 1x for the wider view. Only use the higher zooms in good light, and rest your phone against the wall so it stays sharp. At the monument, zoom 1x fits the boots and fortress together, and zoom 0.5x with a crouch makes the boots look huge.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the boots, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour at sunset.
card.best_time: Go for sunset at the Baluarte de Santo Domingo, when the warm golden light turns the whole scene orange. The boots look small from up there, so think of them as one part of a sunset picture, not the star.
card.selfie_here: On the Baluarte de Santo Domingo, turn on the front camera and put your back to the city wall's edge so the boots, the sea and the sunset sit behind you. For another sunset selfie, try the wall-top terrace at Café del Mar on the city walls, which looks down on the monument. Check both spots on the ground, since the boots will be small and distant.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back from the boots so the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas rises behind the whole sculpture, while you stand beside the boots.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep an eye on your belongings, because some reviewers mention street vendors and petty theft at the monument. Keep your phone in a pocket or on a wrist strap when you lean in close. Check the official site for local rules before you go, including on flying drones.
card.challenge: Crouch down, switch to zoom 0.5x, and get both boots and the castle in one shot, with the lying boot pointing the eye toward the upright one.
card.good_to_know: The boots honour the Colombian poet Luis Carlos López, who compared Cartagena to a pair of old boots in his poem A mi Ciudad Nativa. Tito Lombana made the first version in enamelled cement in 1957. It was demolished in 1992 to make way for the Heredia Bridge, and his brother Hector Lombana rebuilt it in bronze in 1994.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Baluarte de Santo Domingo, the fortification walkway to the west, about 1.8 km away from the boots, and face east toward the monument and the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas. For the close-up, walk to the boots themselves in Getsemaní, near Media Luna, and shoot with the fortress behind them.

selfie_research.notes: Sources disagree on the location. Access Travel says the monument is on Calle de la Media Luna and in Getsemaní, and Airial says Manga. Wikipedia says the original stood at Media Luna and was rebuilt in bronze in 1994. Tripadvisor and Airial place it at Calle 31 #18B-55, next to San Felipe Castle, which matches your coordinates. One Access Travel page also says it stands in Plaza de los Coches, which I could not confirm elsewhere. None of the pages I found says a visitor can stand with the boots directly behind them, so both selfie spots are inferred from the viewpoint descriptions and should be checked on the ground. No page I found states rules about selfie sticks or tripods.
